newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Timebomb ticks after Belgian scandal compromise.
newsitem.headline: Timebomb ticks after Belgian scandal compromise.

text.p: A parliamentary commission set a bomb ticking under Belgium's coalition government on Thursday by deferring a recommendation on the future of Deputy Prime Minister Elio Di Rupo, accused of having sex with under-age boys.
The compromise, struck after a 16-hour meeting which exposed rifts in the coalition, leaves Di Rupo -- a discreet gay -- waiting for two more weeks confronting the allegations, which he hotly denies.

At the end of that period, with more information at its disposal from the Brussels public prosecutor, the commission will have to decide whether to recommend the full parliament to lift Di Rupo's immunity from prosecution and send him before the Cour de Cassation -- Belgium's highest court.

If that happens he will almost automatically be forced to resign. Even if the case is thrown out he has been politically weakened -- perhaps mortally wounded, although so far its is only opposition politicians who are openly calling for his head.
But it is not only the fate of Di Rupo, a francophone socialist, that hangs in the balance.

The commission's decision, which must be endorsed by the full parliament later on Thursday, was reached only after Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene put pressure on his own Christian Democratic Party (CVP) to support Di Rupo.

Dehaene's action prompted the newspaper La Libre Belgique to describe him as "a prime minister who cancelled a visit to his counterpart in Austria, preferring to dedicate all his efforts to saving his colleague, even his government".
"Whatever happens between now and December 9 the Socialist Party and even Prime Minister Dehaene will be on the defensive," RTBF radio commented.
Belgium's coalition government consists of the francophone and Flemish christian democratic and socialist parties.
The real risk is that rifts revealed between the seven coalition representatives on the 11-member commission will be translated into ruptures in the government itself.

It is a possibility few can desire with the whole political and judicial establishment already under fire for ineptitude and suspicions of corruption after the discovery of an unrelated paedophile abduction and murder scandal three months ago.

The arrest in mid-August of convicted child rapist Marc Dutroux, the subsequent rescue of two sexually abused young girls from a house he owned and the discovery of the bodies of four more girls has shattered public confidence in the system.
Another parliamentary commission is examining the investigations into the six cases and those of at least seven other missing children.

"Is someone trying to bring down the government to prevent the Dutroux Commission completing its task? This case is not purely politics," the newspaper Le Soir quoted an unnamed member of the Dutroux Commission as saying.

Last month 250,000 people took to the streets of Brussels for a march that was intended to show support for the victims of sexual abuse and their parents but rapidly turned into a demonstration of disgust with what is seen as a corrupt system.

Last week the parents of two of the murdered young girls called for the resignation of Interior Minister Johan Vande Lanotte, holding him responsible for bungling by the gendarmerie and threatening to call another mass rally if he refused.
The march, if it took place, could turn ugly given the mood in the country, observers said.
